{#xmca} At the cutoff date (2025 September 30), the median follow-up for all patients was 24.3 months (interquartile range 6.6 to 44.4 months). In our study, the 1-year PFS rate was 54.2%, exceeding the prespecified target. The 1.5-year and 2-year PFS rates were 42.2% and 28.6%, respectively, with a median PFS of 16.1 months (95% CI 11.4 to 19.2 months; Fig. 1G). The 1-year and 2-year OS rates were 83.1% and 57.7%, respectively, and the median OS was 29.3 months (95% CI 21.9 months to not reached; Fig. 1H). The ORR and DCR were 69.9% (58/83; 95% CI 58.8% to 79.5%) and 91.6% (76/83; 95% CI 83.4% to 96.5%), respectively (Fig. 2A and B). A total of 14 patients (16.9%) were downstaged to stage III and received hypofractionated radiotherapy. Among the remaining 69 patients, median PFS was 16.8 months (95% CI 11.3 to 19.2 months), and median OS was 24.0 months (95% CI 21.2 to 25.4 months). No statistically significant differences in PFS (*P* = 0.57; Fig. S1A) or OS (*P* = 0.45; Fig. S1B) were observed between the 14 patients who were downstaged to stage III and the remaining 69 patients. A total of 32 patients (38.6%) had distant metastasis beyond radiotherapy lesions, and 9 patients (10.8%) experienced both radiotherapy lesion progression and distant metastasis. Additionally, 20 patients (24.1%) experienced progression of LDRT lesions only, whereas no SABR lesions progressed (Table S6)*.*

{#j48m} **Background:** Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based chemoimmunotherapy has become a standard first-line treatment for patients with driver-negative metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but the clinical benefit is limited. Radiotherapy has potential antitumor immunomodulatory effects, but the optimal dose and fractionation remain unclear. **Methods:** This single-arm, multicenter, prospective, phase II trial enrolled patients with stage IV driver-negative NSCLC who received first-line chemoimmunotherapy. During the ICI maintenance phase, patients received hybrid dose-fraction radiotherapy (Hybrid-RT): stereotactic ablative body radiotherapy (SABR) to targetable lesions and low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) to other sites. {#yxdx} This prospective, multicenter phase II study evaluated the efficacy and safety of ICI combined with Hybrid-RT in patients with metastatic driver gene-negative NSCLC. Hybrid-RT is selected based on individual lesions. It adopts a dose-fractionation regimen characterized by short-course, low-total-dose radiotherapy. This approach theoretically reduces toxicity to organs at risk and minimizes radiation-induced immunosuppression, making it more suitable for combination with ICI therapy [@w:w20]. The study met its primary endpoint, with a 1-year PFS rate of 54.2% and a median PFS of 16.1 months, representing clinically meaningful and highly promising outcomes.

{#r1hz} # Discussion

{#yxdx} This prospective, multicenter phase II study evaluated the efficacy and safety of ICI combined with Hybrid-RT in patients with metastatic driver gene-negative NSCLC. Hybrid-RT is selected based on individual lesions. It adopts a dose-fractionation regimen characterized by short-course, low-total-dose radiotherapy. This approach theoretically reduces toxicity to organs at risk and minimizes radiation-induced immunosuppression, making it more suitable for combination with ICI therapy [@w:w20]. The study met its primary endpoint, with a 1-year PFS rate of 54.2% and a median PFS of 16.1 months, representing clinically meaningful and highly promising outcomes.

{#z6y4} In this trial, radiotherapy was administered during ICI maintenance after chemoimmunotherapy. Platinum-based chemoimmunotherapy achieves maximal tumor response in the induction phase but carries substantial toxicity. Thus, most novel ICI combinations are increasingly investigated in the maintenance setting [@w:w21]. Our sequential design was rationally constructed to avoid additive toxicity from concurrent chemo-immunoradiotherapy and minimize target volumes by delivering focal radiotherapy in the setting of reduced tumor burden. This optimized treatment sequence appears to account for both the promising survival efficacy and the favorable safety outcomes.

{#uuvi} # Background

{#mjmh} Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) comprises heterogeneous pathological subtypes and molecular profiles . From a molecular and therapeutic perspective, NSCLC can be broadly categorized into 2 groups: driver gene-positive and driver gene-negative. While immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have provided substantial clinical benefit to patients with driver gene-negative tumors, a substantial proportion of those with advanced disease still do not achieve long-term survival [@w:w1]. Therefore, overcoming immune resistance remains a major therapeutic challenge.

{#pjv0} Radiotherapy plays a role in the treatment of NSCLC at almost all stages. Accumulating clinical evidence has demonstrated synergism between radiotherapy and immunotherapy [@w:w2], whereby radiotherapy enhances the efficacy of ICIs in both early- and advanced-stage NSCLC [@w:w3]. Preclinical studies indicate that radiotherapy promotes antitumor immunity by inducing immunogenic cell death (ICD) and remodeling the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). The core mechanism by which radiotherapy exerts antitumor effects involves ionizing radiation-induced DNA damage, which activates ICD pathways. This can convert irradiated tumor cells into an in situ tumor vaccine, triggering systemic antitumor responses in nonirradiated distant lesions, a phenomenon known as the abscopal effect [@w:w4].
